<backstage_guidance>
The induction is finished. Recent passages keep proving that the loan cupboard is locked, permissions are observed, and nobody is imposing on Rowan. Those facts are already secure. Maintain them as background; spend words on them again only when something changes or they affect a present choice. The narrator should describe what happens, without explaining how it respects Rowan's boundaries or what an absent demand means.

Work can remain work. Select details for their particular interest and what they let us experience, rather than recording every safe handling step. A requested time skip should reach its endpoint; a live exchange should leave room for a reply. Do not compensate for a quiet morning by arranging a compulsory encounter or a new problem.

The early supper gave nearly everyone polished rejoinders; the induction then made Nell an instruction manual. Let speech follow the speaker's immediate purpose and relationship with the listener. Plain answers, unfinished exchanges, particular pleasures and unreturned jokes can carry distinct voices. Do not explain the psychology afterwards. A refusal can be accepted without making its acceptance a speech.

There is no need to repair compatible invented details or recite these corrections in the fiction. Keep the established knowledge boundaries, ownership of player choices and real consequences.

Choose Owen's interview as the main developing personal thread for the next day. He wants this opportunity and intends to accept before Wednesday noon. His Thursday-to-Friday swap is approved in principle; the written request and Nell's confirmation still need to happen. Let him take those steps himself. His difficulty is telling Martin what the opportunity means when Martin has begun imagining a settled future together at the cinema. Give that relationship room to change through something Owen or Martin actually does. Do not assume an interview result or a decision to leave town.

This is direction for future action, not a report that these things have happened. Rowan and Nell know only about an inland appointment; Jo knows the interview, and Martin has not been told. A disclosure must come from someone who can make it. If Rowan meets Owen, Owen can decide what he wants to share; do not make the encounter or a confession compulsory. Offstage decisions can become visible later through their consequences, without a report of every private conversation.

Let the reopening also mean a life people want to have. Jo wants time with Fran and misses Ines; Nell wants the booked walking weekend with Gina. Their immediate business can reveal a preference or decision serving those lives, rather than only another duty. If Bea is naturally at lunch, her answer can draw on the films, possessions and people she cares about. They need not all appear, and Rowan need not help. Use the full histories to choose what matters to the people who are actually present.

Resolve the existing practical clock: Dev's Tuesday evening hold required confirmation by noon today. Establish the outcome consistently if it becomes relevant; Rosa's completed photographs and her evening with Beth do not need to be disrupted. These are opportunities for independent progress, not errands for Rowan or a required sequence of scenes.
</backstage_guidance>

Return the next passage of fiction.

At lunch, if Bea is present, I ask what she enjoys about having the cinema open again. If she is not here, I eat with whoever is around.

summary: **Assigning Jo’s weekday off for family time**
**Confirming Owen's shift request and invite status**

item.text:
When you come downstairs, Bea is at one of the cafe tables with Nell, Jo and Owen. She has brought a cheese sandwich, an apple and a small jar of pickled walnuts. Jo is drinking black coffee beside a sheet of pencilled menu costs.

Owen stands at the end of the table with a folded note.

“Thursday moved to Friday,” he tells Nell. “Same hours. Ten till four.”

Nell reads it, opens the staff rota and moves his name into Friday’s column.

“That’s confirmed. I’ll email you a copy this afternoon.”

“Thanks.”

He sits down with his lunch. Martin is not here to hear the exchange, and nobody asks Owen about the inland appointment.

You take a place at the table. With Bea present, you ask, “What do you enjoy about having the cinema open again?”

She considers this while adding two pickled walnuts to her sandwich.

“The sign,” she says first. “We spent more on restoring it than I was comfortable putting in the budget. Then I approved it anyway. I’ve wanted to see it lit again since the place closed.”

Nell glances up from the rota. “Martin’s testing the lamps after dark.”

“He’s already warned me that one may be the wrong shade of white.”

Bea closes her sandwich and continues. “My granddaughter’s coming in October, too. We send each other terrible films on secondhand discs. She writes categories on the cases. Worst wig. Least convincing monster. Things like that.”

“She’s very systematic,” Jo says.

“Only when the film is bad. I want to bring her here and let her choose something we can complain about together.”

Bea takes a bite, then looks across the foyer towards the locked auditorium.

“And I want this to become ordinary again. Not another fundraiser, not people coming in because they’ve been asked to save the building. Someone finishes work, sees what’s on and buys a ticket. That part.”

“And coffee,” Jo says.

Bea reaches for her apple without answering the addition.
